title: Newton's laws and forces
note: A net force changes velocity; it is not needed to keep velocity. Newton's second law, F_net = ma, uses the vector sum of all external forces on one object. Third-law pairs are equal and opposite but act on different objects, so they never cancel each other in a free-body diagram.

read.title: Forces change motion
text: For two thousand years many thinkers assumed that moving things need a push to keep going. Newton's first law says the opposite: an object keeps moving at constant velocity unless a net force acts on it. A hockey puck slows down because of friction, not because motion naturally fades. The property that resists changes in motion is inertia, and mass measures it.

The second law makes this quantitative: the net external force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration. The word net matters. A car cruising at steady speed on a straight road has forces acting on it, but they balance, so its acceleration and net force are both zero.

The third law says forces always come in pairs. If Earth pulls you down with your weight, you pull Earth up with an equal force. The floor pushing up on you is a different force, the normal force, and it is not the partner of your weight. Third-law partners act on different objects, so they never appear together on one free-body diagram.
To solve a problem, isolate one object, draw every external force on it, choose axes, and apply F_net = ma along each axis.
